To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the anisotropies of cosmic rays in the energy range from 1 to 10 TeV and the spectra of electrons in the same energy range can be described by one set of sources.

the experimental data on the phase and amplitude energy dependences of cosmic ray proton (p) anisotropy in the energy range 1-10 TeV and the electron spectra in the range 1-20 TeV are described within one set of sources, which are supernovae (SN) in the Galaxy, the nearest 100 pc from us, and SN remnants (SNR) in our Galaxy.
the phase of the proton anisotropies in the 1 to 10 TeV range is well described by the time of the supernova explosion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible explanation of the experimental results on CR proton anisotropies and electron spectra in terms of a single nearby source model.
a possible contribution of nearby sources to CRs in the 1–TeV range, the time dependence of which is taken into account.
the problem of the origin of CRs with energies of 1 TeV and higher, which are the main source of galactic radiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anisotropies of protons and electrons at 1 TeV can be explained by the contribution of nearby sources.

the anisotropies of cosmic rays in the 1 GeV-1 TeV range and the spectra of electrons in the 1-Tev range can be described within one set of sources, if the contribution of nearby sources is taken into account.

the observed CR proton anisotropies in the energy range from 1 to 10 TeV and the electron spectra in the energy range 10-1000 TeV are determined by the contribution of nearby sources, and the contribution of more distant sources can be neglected in this energy range.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the anisotropies and spectra of cosmic ray protons and electrons in the 1–10 TeV range can be described in terms of the same nearby sources.

the contribution of nearby supernovae is not excluded as a source of electrons in the 1 - TeV energy range, although the contribution of electrons emitted from magnetospheres of young pulsars cannot be excluded either.
the contribution from nearby sources to CRs in the 1–100 TeV range is determined with an accuracy of 10–20%, which is much better than that obtained in our previous works.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the anisotropies and electron spectra in this range are determined by the same nearby sources, while the contribution of the pulsars to the electron spectra is small and is not more than 10% of the total intensity.
the contribution from nearby pulsars to the 1-GeV CR electron flux can reach 30-50% and that this contribution can be determined by the amplitude and phase anisotropy data.
the anisotropies in the CR electron and proton spectra are caused by the same set of nearby sources, which are mainly supernova remnants.
